claim: CARM1 is a cancer-relevant protein arginine methyltransferase that regulates many aspects of transcription.
source: CARM1 is a cancer-relevant protein arginine methyltransferase that regulates many aspects of transcription.
evidence: This is a general statement about CARM1 function supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: SKI-73 (6a) can rapidly penetrate cell membranes and then be processed into active inhibitors.
source: SKI-73 (6a) can rapidly penetrate cell membranes and then be processed into active inhibitors, which are retained intracellularly with 10-fold enrichment for several days.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing cellular uptake and processing of SKI-73.

claim: Active inhibitors derived from SKI-73 (6a) are retained intracellularly with 10-fold enrichment for several days.
source: SKI-73 (6a) can rapidly penetrate cell membranes and then be processed into active inhibitors, which are retained intracellularly with 10-fold enrichment for several days.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS quantification data showing intracellular accumulation.

claim: SKI-73 (6a) recapitulates the effect of CARM1 knockout against breast cancer cell invasion.
source: SKI-73 (6a) recapitulates the effect of CARM1 knockout against breast cancer cell invasion.
evidence: This is supported by invasion assay data comparing SKI-73 treatment with CARM1-KO cells.

claim: The SKI-73(6a)-associated reduction of invasiveness acts by altering epigenetic plasticity and suppressing the invasion-prone subpopulation.
source: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis revealed that the SKI-73(6a)-associated reduction of invasiveness acts by altering epigenetic plasticity and suppressing the invasion-prone subpopulation.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis data.

claim: SKI-73 (6a) and CARM1 knockout alter the epigenetic plasticity with remarkable difference.
source: Interestingly, SKI-73 (6a) and CARM1 knockout alter the epigenetic plasticity with remarkable difference, suggesting distinct modes of action for small-molecule and genetic perturbations.
evidence: This is supported by comparative scRNA-seq analysis of SKI-73 treated and CARM1-KO cells.

claim: Many PMTs are implicated as vulnerable targets against cancer malignancy.
source: Many PMTs are implicated as vulnerable targets against cancer malignancy (Kaniskan et al., 2018; Luo, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CARM1 regulates multiple aspects of transcription by methylating diverse targets including RNAPII, SRC3, C/EBPβ, PAX3/7, SOX2/9, RUNX1, Notch1, p300, CBP, p/CIP, Med12, and BAF155.
source: Among the important Type I PRMTs is CARM1 (PRMT4), which regulates multiple aspects of transcription by methylating diverse targets including RNAPII, SRC3, C/EBPβ, PAX3/7, SOX2/9, RUNX1, Notch1, p300, CBP, p/CIP, Med12, and BAF155 (Blanc and Richard, 2017; Hein et al., 2015; Vu et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2014a; Yang and Bedford, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The requirement of CARM1 is implicated in multiple cancers, with its methyltransferase activity particularly addicted by hematopoietic malignancies and metastatic breast cancer.
source: The requirement of CARM1 is implicated in multiple cancers, with its methyltransferase activity particularly addicted by hematopoietic malignancies and metastatic breast cancer (Drew et al., 2017; Greenblatt et al., 2018; Nakayama et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CARM1 methylates Arg1064 of BAF155 and thus facilitates the recruitment of the BAF155-containing SWI/SNF complex to a specific subset of gene loci that are essential for breast cancer metastasis.
source: Mechanistically, CARM1 methylates Arg1064 of BAF155 and thus facilitates the recruitment of the BAF155-containing SWI/SNF complex to a specific subset of gene loci that are essential for breast cancer metastasis.
evidence: This is supported by prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: EZM2302, TP-064 and SKI-73 (6a) are the only selective and cell-active CARM1 chemical probes.
source: To the best of our knowledge, EZM2302 (Drew et al., 2017; Greenblatt et al., 2018), TP-064 (Nakayama et al., 2018) and SKI-73 (6a in this work, www.thesgc.org/chemical-probes/SKI-73), which were developed by Epizyme, Takeda/SGC(Structural Genomic Consortium), and our team, respectively, are the only selective and cell-active CARM1 chemical probes.
evidence: This is based on a review of the literature and knowledge of the field.

claim: 6′-homosinefungin (HSF, 1) binds to the Type I PRMTs (PRMT1, CARM1, PRMT6 and PRMT8) with IC50 of 13‒300 nM.
source: As a SAM mimic, 1 binds to the Type I PRMTs (namely PRMT1, CARM1, PRMT6 and PRMT8) with IC50 of 13‒300 nM (Figure 1a,c, Supplementary file 1-Table A).
evidence: This is supported by IC50 assay data presented in Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1-Table A.

claim: The relative affinity of 1 to Type I PRMTs aligns with that of the SAM mimics SAH and SNF (around 20-fold lower IC50 of 1 versus SAH and SNF).
source: Its relative affinity to Type I PRMTs aligns with that of the SAM mimics SAH and SNF (around 20-fold lower IC50 of 1 versus SAH and SNF, Figure 1a,c, Supplementary file 1-Table A).
evidence: This is supported by comparative IC50 data in Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1-Table A.

claim: HSF derivative 2a binds preferentially to CARM1 with IC50 = 30 ± 3 nM and >10 fold selectivity over other seven human PRMTs and 26 methyltransferases of other classes.
source: The HSF derivative 2a (Figure 1b) was identified for its preferential binding to CARM1 with IC50 = 30 ± 3 nM and >10 fold selectivity over other seven human PRMTs and 26 methyltransferases of other classes (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1-Table A).
evidence: This is supported by IC50 assay data presented in Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1-Table A.

claim: Compound 5a shows an IC50 of 43 ± 7 nM against CARM1 and a >10-fold selectivity over the panel of 33 diverse methyltransferases.
source: Here, 5a shows an IC50 of 43 ± 7 nM against CARM1 and a >10-fold selectivity over the panel of 33 diverse methyltransferases (Figure 1c, Supplementary file 1-Table A).
evidence: This is supported by IC50 assay data presented in Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1-Table A.

claim: The Kd values of 2a and 5a are Kd,2a = 17 ± 8 nM and Kd,5a = 9 ± 5 nM.
source: The Kd values of 2a and 5a (Kd,2a = 17 ± 8 nM; Kd,5a = 9 ± 5 nM) were extrapolated from the y-axis intercepts upon fitting the equation IC50 = [SAM]×Kd/Km,SAM+Kd (Figure 2b) (Segel, 1993).
evidence: This is derived from experimental data in Figure 2b using a standard equation.

claim: The presence of the H3 peptide substrate had negligible effect on the binding of 2a and 5a, indicating their substrate-noncompetitive character.
source: By contrast, the presence of the H3 peptide substrate had negligible effect on the binding of 2a and 5a, indicating their substrate-noncompetitive character (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2c.

claim: The SAM analogs 2a and 5a were characterized as SAM-competitive, substrate-noncompetitive inhibitors of CARM1.
source: The SAM analogs 2a and 5a were thus characterized as SAM-competitive, substrate-noncompetitive inhibitors of CARM1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2b and 2c.

claim: SPR analysis showed biphasic binding of 2a and 5a to CARM1 with Ki1,2a = 56 nM and Ki2,2a = 404 nM; Ki1,5a = 105 nM and Ki2,5a = 541 nM.
source: The SPR signal progression of 2a and 5a fits with a biphasic rather than a mono-phasic binding mode, with the lower Ki1,2a = 0.06 ± 0.02 µM, Ki1,5a = 0.10 ± 0.01 µM, and the higher Ki2,5b = 0.54 ± 0.07 µM, Ki2,2a = 0.4 ± 0.1 µM, probably because of the multi-phase binding kinetics of 2a and 5a (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by SPR experimental data in Figure 2d.

claim: The binding of 2a and 5a (at 5 μM concentration) increased the melting temperature (Tm) of CARM1 by 4.4°C and 6.5°C, respectively.
source: The binding of 2a and 5a (at 5 μM concentration) increased the melting temperature (Tm) of CARM1 by 4.4°C and 6.5°C, respectively (Figure 2e, Tm, 2a = 44.2 ± 0.4 °C and Tm, 5a = 46.3 ± 0.3 °C versus Tm, DMSO = 39.8 ± 0.3 °C as control).
evidence: This is supported by thermal shift assay data in Figure 2e.

claim: The X-ray structure of CARM1 in complex with 5a was solved with resolution of 2.00 Å.
source: To further seek a structural rationale for 5a and 2a for CARM1 inhibition, we solved the X-ray structure of CARM1 in complex with 5a with resolution of 2.00 Å and modeled the CARM1 binding of 2a (Figure 3, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: 5a adopts a noncanonical pose with its 6′-N-benzyl moiety in a binding pocket that used to be occupied by the α-amino carboxylate moiety of canonical ligands such as SAH, SNF and 1.
source: However, 5a adopts a noncanonical pose with its 6′-N-benzyl moiety in a binding pocket that used to be occupied by the α-amino carboxylate moiety of canonical ligands such as SAH, SNF and 1 (Figures 3c and 4), while the α-amino methoxyphenethyl amide moiety of 5a protrudes into the substrate-binding pocket (Boriack-Sjodin et al., 2016; Sack et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the X-ray structure in Figure 3c.

claim: Treatment of MCF-7 cells with 10 µM of 6a fully suppressed the Arg1064 methylation of BAF155, whereas treatment with 2a and 5a did not affect this mark.
source: Treatment of MCF-7 cells with 10 µM of 6a fully suppressed this methylation mark, whereas treatment with 2a and 5a did not affect this mark (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5b.

claim: 6a can be efficiently processed into 2a inside cells.
source: Intracellularly, 6a can be processed into 5a and 2a.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS quantification data in Figure 5c.

claim: >100 μM of 2a can be accumulated inside cells for 2 days after 6 hr treatment with a single dose of 5‒10 µM 6a.
source: Remarkably, >100 μM of 2a can be accumulated inside cells for 2 days after 6 hr treatment with a single dose of 5‒10 µM 6a.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS quantification data in Figure 5c.

claim: The intracellular concentration of SAM was determined to be 89 ± 16 µM.
source: The SAM cofactor, whose intracellular concentration was determined to be 89 ± 16 µM (Figure 5c,d), is expected to occupy >99.5% CARM1 with residual <0.5% as the apo-enzyme under a native setting.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS quantification data in Figure 5c.

claim: With single doses of 6a of 2.5‒10 µM, the combined CARM1 occupancy by 2a, 5a and their pro-drug precursor 6a rapidly reached the plateau of >95% within 6 hr, and was maintained at this level for at least 48 hr.
source: With single doses of 6a of 2.5‒10 µM, the combined CARM1 occupancy by 2a, 5a and their pro-drug precursor 6a rapidly reached the plateau of >95% within 6 hr, and was maintained at this level for at least 48 hr (Figure 5e, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on modeling using LC-MS/MS data and Kd values, presented in Figure 5e.

claim: The treatment of MDA-MB-231 cells with 6a but with not the control compound 6b increased cellular Tm and thus the thermal stability of CARM1 by 4.3 ± 0.6°C.
source: Our data showed that the treatment of MDA-MB-231 cells with 6a but with not the control compound 6b increased cellular Tm and thus the thermal stability of CARM1 by 4.3 ± 0.6°C (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by CETSA data in Figure 5f.

claim: The Arg1064 methylation of BAF155 and the Arg455/Arg460 methylation of PABP1 can be fully suppressed by 6a in a dose-dependent manner.
source: These methylation marks can be fully suppressed by 6a in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 6a.

claim: The EC50 values for suppression of BAF155 and PABP1 methylation by 6a are 0.45‒0.75 µM.
source: The resultant EC50 values of 0.45‒0.75 µM (Figure 6b) are well correlated with the modeled 60% cellular occupancy of CARM1 upon treatment with 0.5 µM 6a for 48 hr (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in Figure 6b.

claim: Treatment with SKI-73 (6a) but not its negative control compound SKI-73N (6b) suppressed the invasion of MDA-MB-231 cells (EC50 = 1.3 µM).
source: Relative to the control treatment with DMSO, treatment with SKI-73 (6a) but not its negative control compound SKI-73N (6b) suppressed the invasion of MDA-MB-231 cells (EC50 = 1.3 µM) (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is supported by invasion assay data in Figure 6c and 6d.

claim: The treatment with ≥10 µM 6a produced the maximal 80% suppression of the invasion by MDA-MB-231 relative to the DMSO control, which is comparable with the phenotype of CARM1-KO.
source: The treatment with ≥10 µM 6a produced the maximal 80% suppression of the invasion by MDA-MB-231 relative to the DMSO control, which is comparable with the phenotype of CARM1-KO (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by invasion assay data in Figure 6e.

claim: No further inhibition by 6a on the invasiveness was observed upon 6a treatment of MDA-MB-231 CARM1-KO cells.
source: Critically, no further inhibition by 6a on the invasiveness was observed upon 6a treatment (in comparison with the treatment with DMSO or 6b treatment) of MDA-MB-231 CARM1-KO cells (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by invasion assay data in Figure 6e.

claim: Treatment with 6a and 6b under the current condition has no apparent impact on the proliferation of parental or CARM1-KO MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Notably, treatment with 6a and 6b under the current condition has no apparent impact on the proliferation of parental or CARM1-KO MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with the intact proliferation upon treatment with other CARM1 chemical probes (Drew et al., 2017; Greenblatt et al., 2018; Nakayama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by MTT assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and by comparison with other CARM1 inhibitors.

claim: 10 × Genomics droplet-based scRNA-seq was conducted on 3232, 3583 and 4099 individual cells (a total of 10,914 cells) exposed to 48 hr treatment with SKI-73 (6a), SKI-73N (6b) and DMSO, respectively.
source: Here we conducted 10 × Genomics droplet-based scRNA-seq of 3232, 3583 and 4099 individual cells (a total of 10,914 cells) exposed to 48 hr treatment with SKI-73 (6a), SKI-73N (6b) and DMSO, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for scRNA-seq.

claim: Individual cells were classified into G0/G1, S, and G2/M stages (6885, 1520 and 2509 cells, respectively).
source: To dissect the subpopulation-associated transcriptomic signatures of invasive cells, we included one additional layer for hierarchical clustering by first classifying the individual cells into G0/G1, S, and G2/M stages (6885, 1520 and 2509 cells, respectively) (Figure 7—figure supplement 6, Supplementary file 1-Table E), and then conducted the unsupervised clustering within each cell-cycle-aware subset (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplements 19–30, Supplementary file 1-Table E).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle scoring data in Figure 7—figure supplement 6.

claim: The cell-cycle-aware algorithm resulted in 21, 7 and 6 subpopulations in G0/G1, S, and G2/M phases, respectively.
source: The cell-cycle-aware algorithm allowed the clustering of these cells according to the three cell cycle stages under the three treatment conditions and resulted in 21, 7 and 6 subpopulations in G0/G1, S, and G2/M phases, respectively (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplements 21, 25 and 29, Supplementary file 1-Tables F–H).
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis presented in Figure 7b and supplementary figures.

claim: The 48 hr treatments with SKI-73 (6a) or SKI-73N (6b) had no effect on the cell cycle.
source: Notably, the 48 hr treatments with SKI-73 (6a) or SKI-73N (6b) had no effect on the cell cycle, as indicated by their comparable cell-cycle distribution patterns (Figure 7—figure supplement 6; Supplementary file 1-Table E), a finding that is consistent with intact proliferation after all three treatments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle distribution data in Figure 7—figure supplement 6 and proliferation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Subpopulation 8 of G0/G1-phase cells is the most sensitive and the only subpopulation that can be depleted by around 80% with SKI-73 (6a) treatment.
source: Subpopulation 8 of G0/G1-phase cells is the most sensitive and the only subpopulation that can be depleted by around 80% with SKI-73 (6a) treatment (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by population analysis data in Figure 7c.

claim: The invasive phenotype of MDA-MB-231 cells predominantly arises from Subpopulation 8 G0/G1-phase cells, which only accounts for ~8% of the parental cells in G0/G1 phase (~5% without cell-cycle awareness).
source: Given the ~80% suppression and ~20% residual invasion capability upon SKI-73 (6a) treatment, we argue that the invasive phenotype of MDA-MB-231 cells predominantly arises from Subpopulation 8 G0/G1-phase cells, which only accounts for ~8% of the parental cells in G0/G1 phase (~5% without cell-cycle awareness).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between invasion suppression and depletion of Subpopulation 8.

claim: Differential expression analysis revealed the single-cell transcriptional signatures of metastasis-implicated genes (e.g. MORC4, S100A2, RPL39, IFI27, ARF6, CHD11, SDPR and KRT18) that are specific for the G0/G1-phase Subpopulation 8 and invasive cells.
source: Differential expression analysis further revealed the single-cell transcriptional signatures of metastasis-implicated genes (e.g. MORC4, S100A2, RPL39, IFI27, ARF6, CHD11, SDPR and KRT18) that are specific for the G0/G1-phase Subpopulation 8 and invasive cells but not for other G0/G1-phase invasion-prone candidates such as Subpopulation 6/7/9/14 (Figure 7e, Figure 7—figure supplement 43, Supplementary file 1-Table L).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis data in Figure 7e and Figure 7—figure supplement 43.

claim: CARM1 knockout or CARM1 inhibition with SKI-73 (6a) alters the epigenetic plasticity in a proliferation-independent manner by replacing the most invasion-prone subpopulation with the non-invasive subpopulation(s) to suppress the invasive phenotype.
source: Collectively, either CARM1 knockout or CARM1 inhibition with SKI-73 (6a) alters the epigenetic plasticity in a proliferation-independent manner by replacing the most invasion-prone subpopulation with the non-invasive subpopulation(s) to suppress the invasive phenotype (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scRNA-seq analysis and invasion assay data.

claim: The X-ray structure of CARM1 in complex with 1 (HSF) was solved with a resolution of 2.00 Å.
source: Given the tight CARM1 binding by 1, we solved the X-ray structure of CARM1 in complex with 1 (HSF) with a resolution of 2.00 Å (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: In the CARM1–1 complex, 1 can adopt four alternative configurations.
source: However, the CARM1–1 complex is distinct for multiple configurations of its ligand and interactions via its 6′-methyleneamine moiety (Figure 4b–d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). In the CARM1–1 complex, 1 can adopt four alternative configurations (Configuration I in Chains B, D; Configuration II in Chain C; Configuration III and IV in Chain A) accompanied with the structural accommodation of the adjacent residues and water hydrogen bonds (Figure 4b–d, Supplementary file 1-Table B–D).
evidence: This is supported by the X-ray structure in Figure 4b-d.

claim: Only a single configuration of the ligands was observed in SAH- or SNF-bound CARM1.
source: By contrast, only a single configuration of the ligands was observed in SAH- or SNF-bound CARM1 (Figure 4c,d, PDB: 2Y1X, 2Y1W) (Sack et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously published crystal structures.

claim: The CARM1–1 complex gains strong hydrogen bonds via the 6′-methyleneamine moiety of the ligand with the backbone carbonyl of CARM1's Glu258 or the side chain of Tyr154.
source: Most noticeably, the CARM1–1 complex gains the strong hydrogen bonds via the 6′-methyleneamine moiety of the ligand with (i) the backbone carbonyl of CARM1's Glu258 (Configuration I, II in Chains B, C, D and Configuration III in Chain A) or (ii) the side chain of Tyr154 (Configuration IV in Chain A), together with several less conserved water hydrogen bonds (Figure 4c,d, Supplementary file 1-Table B–D).
evidence: This is supported by the X-ray structure in Figure 4c,d.

claim: The 6′-amine of SNF in the CARM1–SNF complex forms weaker hydrogen bonds with Glu258 and may fewer water hydrogen bonds compared to 1.
source: By contrast, the 6′-amine of SNF in the CARM1–SNF complex forms weaker hydrogen bonds with Glu258 and may fewer water hydrogen bonds (Figure 4c, Supplementary file 1-Table B, C, PDB: 2Y1W).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the CARM1-1 structure with the CARM1-SNF structure.

claim: Comparable interactions are completely absent from the CARM1–SAH complex.
source: Comparable interactions are completely absent from the CARM1–SAH complex (Figure 4d, Supplementary file 1-Table B–D, PDB: 2Y1X).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the CARM1-SAH structure.

claim: The desired hydrogen-bond networks of the 6′-methyleneamine moiety of 1 with CARM1 can rationalize the significant decrease of IC50 from SNF and SAH to 1.
source: The desired hydrogen-bond networks of the 6′-methyleneamine moiety of 1 with CARM1, which are present in the CARM1-1 complex but absent from the CARM1–SNF and CARM1–SAH complexes, can rationalize the significant decrease of IC50 from SNF and SAH to 1.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison and IC50 data.

claim: In Chains A and C of the CARM1–1 complex, the carboxylate moiety of the ligand forms an ionic bond with Arg169 and a hydrogen bond with Gln160.
source: In Chains A and C of the CARM1–1 complex, the carboxylate moiety of the ligand forms an ionic bond with Arg169 and a hydrogen bond with Gln160 (Figure 4b,c,d, Supplementary file 1-Table B, C).
evidence: This is supported by the X-ray structure in Figure 4b,c,d.

claim: Such interactions are absent from CARM1–SNF and CARM1–SAH complexes.
source: Such interactions are absent from CARM1–SNF and CARM1–SAH complexes (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: In Chains B and D of the CARM1–1 complex, the carboxylate moiety forms ionic bonds with Arg169 and a water hydrogen bond.
source: By contrast, in Chains B and D of the CARM1–1 complex, the same carboxylate moiety forms the ionic bonds with Arg169 and a water hydrogen bond (Figure 4b,c,d, Supplementary file 1-Table B, C).
evidence: This is supported by the X-ray structure in Figure 4b,c,d.

claim: The general high affinity of 1, SNF and SAH arises from the combined hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions of these ligands with CARM1.
source: Collectively, the general high affinity of 1, SNF and SAH (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1-Table B–D) arises from the combined hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions of these ligands with CARM1.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: In comparison with SNF and SAH, 1 gains the extra interactions via its 6′-methyleneamine moiety.
source: However, in comparison with SNF and SAH, 1 gains the extra interactions via its 6′-methyleneamine moiety (Figure 4c,d, Supplementary file 1-Table B–D).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison in Figure 4c,d.

claim: 1 adopts the canonical pose with its α-amino carboxylate moiety interacting with Arg168, which is similar to that of SNF and SAH but different from the noncanonical pose of 2a and 5a, upon binding CARM1.
source: In addition, 1 adopts the canonical pose with its α-amino carboxylate moiety interacting with Arg168, which is similar to that of SNF and SAH but different from the noncanonical pose of 2a and 5a, upon binding CARM1 (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison in Figure 4d.

claim: 6a showed decent metabolic stability with 24% residual 6a after one-hour incubation with rat liver microsomes.
source: In the presence of rat liver microsomes, 6a showed decent stability with 24% residual 6a after one-hour incubation.
evidence: This is supported by microsomal stability assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The conversion of 6a into 5a accounted for 40% of the microsome-processed 6a; no production of 2a was detected.
source: Here, the conversion of 6a into 5a accounted for 40% of the microsome-processed 6a; no production of 2a was detected.
evidence: This is supported by microsomal stability assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: 6b can penetrate cell membranes and be processed into 5b and 2b in a similar manner as 6a.
source: Here, 6b can penetrate cell membranes and be processed into 5b and 2b in a similar manner as 6a (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: The pharmacological inhibition of CARM1 by SKI-73 (6a) recapitulates the anti-invasion effect of the genetic perturbation of CARM1.
source: The pharmacological inhibition of CARM1 by SKI-73 (6a) recapitulates the anti-invasion effect of the genetic perturbation of CARM1.
evidence: This is supported by invasion assay data comparing SKI-73 treatment with CARM1-KO.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CARM1 alters epigenetic plasticity and suppresses invasion by suppressing the most invasive subpopulation of breast cancer cells.
source: Our scRNA-seq analysis provides the unprecedented insight that pharmacological inhibition of CARM1 alters epigenetic plasticity and suppresses invasion by suppressing the most invasive subpopulation of breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from scRNA-seq analysis and invasion assay data.
